heroIntro: Every year across Bangladesh, hundreds of thousands of aspiring workers and youth dream of securing employment in Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Malaysia, Italy, or Eastern Europe to build a secure future for their families. Tragically, this migration desperation is exploited by predatory manpower syndicates, unlicensed sub-agents (Dalals), and rogue recruiting agencies. Victims sell ancestral lands, borrow money at exorbitant interest, and hand over BDT 5,00,000 to BDT 15,00,000 for promised high-paying jobs, only to receive fake tourist visas, face severe exploitation abroad, or find themselves abandoned in transit camps in Dubai or Libya. In Bangladesh, taking money under false promises of foreign employment is not a mere civil breach of contract—it constitutes severe, non-bailable criminal offenses under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 and the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013, punishable by life imprisonment. Here is the comprehensive legal guide to prosecuting visa fraudsters, opposing bail, and recovering stolen funds.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: What Legal Action Can You Take Against a Fraudulent Visa Agent (Dalal) in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: When an agent or agency takes money under false promises of foreign employment and fails to send the worker, provides fake visas, or traffics them into forced labor, the victim can take immediate criminal action under two powerful statutes: the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 (Manob Pachar Protirodh O Daman Ain) and the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013. Under Section 3 and Section 7 of the 2012 Act, fraudulent overseas recruitment constitutes human trafficking, which is a cognizable and non-bailable offense carrying penalties from seven (7) years to life imprisonment plus heavy monetary fines. Victims can file an FIR at the local Thana, lodge a complaint directly before the specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal, and submit a formal claim before the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) to seize the recruiting agency's security deposit for full financial compensation.
highlights: Fraudulent overseas employment promises constitute human trafficking under the 2012 Act.
Offenses under the Human Trafficking Act are strictly non-bailable, carrying up to life imprisonment.
Specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunals exist across all 64 districts in Bangladesh.
Victims can recover compensation directly from recruiting agency security deposits through BMET.
points: Step 1: Secure all physical and digital evidence (passports, money receipts, bank deposit slips, WhatsApp chats).
Step 2: Submit a formal complaint to the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) against the recruiting agency.
Step 3: File an FIR at the local Thana under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012.
Step 4: If police delay, file a direct petition before the Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal to issue arrest warrants.

sections.title: The Scourge of Overseas Visa Fraud in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Remittances sent by Bangladeshi migrant workers constitute a primary pillar of the national economy. Yet, the migration corridor remains fraught with deception. Unscrupulous middlemen operating out of rural villages and urban recruitment hubs routinely deceive aspiring workers with promises of 'free visas,' 'direct government work permits,' or 'guaranteed European factory jobs.'

Workers borrow money against high-interest informal loans or sell ancestral farmland to pay sums ranging from BDT 4,00,000 to BDT 12,00,000. Once the funds are pocketed, the brokers deliver counterfeit visas, send workers on tourist visas that result in immediate airport deportation, or route them through illegal transit networks where they face kidnapping and torture in transit countries. When victims demand their money back, brokers respond with threats, claiming political protection. Understanding that modern statutory enactments classify overseas job deception as serious human trafficking is the critical key to bringing these syndicates to justice.

sections.title: Prevention of Human Trafficking Act 2012: Core Provisions
sections.content:
The premier statutory instrument combating cross-border recruitment fraud is the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 (Manob Pachar Protirodh O Daman Ain 2012). The Act provides an expansive statutory definition of trafficking that specifically captures fraudulent foreign employment schemes.

Under Section 3 of the Act, trafficking includes recruiting, transporting, transferring, harboring, or receiving a person for the purpose of exploitation by means of threat, force, fraud, deception, or abuse of power. Section 7 prescribes severe punishments: whoever commits human trafficking shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven (7) years and may extend to life imprisonment, and with fine which shall not be less than five lakh taka (BDT 5,00,000). Furthermore, under Section 8, any person who attempts, abets, or conspires to commit trafficking faces identical rigorous sentences. Offenses under this Act are cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable.

sections.title: Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013: Licensing Rules
sections.content:
Operating parallel to criminal trafficking laws is the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013, which regulates the licensing and operations of recruiting agencies in Bangladesh. The Act makes it a severe criminal offense for any individual or agency to recruit or attempt to send migrant workers abroad without a valid recruiting license issued by the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

Under Section 31 of the 2013 Act, carrying out overseas recruitment without a valid license is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for up to five (5) years and heavy fines. Under Section 33, publishing false advertisements or making fraudulent representations regarding foreign jobs carries imprisonment for up to seven (7) years. Crucially, the Act empowers the government to cancel the operating license of any recruiting agency and forfeit their mandatory security deposit (typically BDT 50,00,000 or more held with the Ministry) to compensate defrauded workers.

sections.title: Essential Evidence: Receipts, Bank Slips, and Chat Logs
sections.content:
To build an impenetrable criminal prosecution against a visa fraudster, documentary and electronic proof must be assembled before confronting the suspect:

  • Financial Audit Trail: Bank deposit slips, cheque counterfoils, RTGS advice, or bKash/Nagad transaction statements showing payments to the broker, agency, or their nominees.
  • Written Agreements and Money Receipts: Any signed money receipt, non-judicial stamp agreement, or handwritten commitment paper signed by the broker acknowledging receipt of funds for foreign employment.
  • Passports and Counterfeit Visas: Photocopies of the victim's passport surrendered to the broker, along with printouts of the fraudulent e-visas, job appointment letters, or fictitious flight tickets.
  • Digital Communications: Audio recordings of phone conversations where the broker promises job placement, and WhatsApp messages detailing visa promises, salary rates, and flight dates.

These exhibits form the core annexures attached to the initial criminal complaint.

sections.title: Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunals: Process and Warrants
sections.content:
To ensure speedy trials, the government established specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunals (Manob Pachar Daman Tribunal) across Bangladesh, presided over by Sessions Judges. Victims have two procedural avenues to institute proceedings:

  1. Filing an FIR at the Thana: The victim lodges a written complaint at the local police station under Sections 7, 8, and 10 of the 2012 Act. Police are mandated to register the FIR, initiate an investigation, and arrest the accused Dalal immediately.
  2. Direct Complaint Petition Before the Tribunal: If the local Thana refuses to register an FIR due to the broker's local influence, an advocate files a Complaint Register (CR) case directly before the Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal. The judge examines the complainant, inspects bank slips, and issues direct arrest warrants or directs the CID or PBI to investigate.

Cases before these specialized tribunals are fast-tracked, putting immense pressure on human trafficking syndicates.

sections.title: BMET Complaints and Agency Security Deposit Claims
sections.content:
In addition to criminal prosecution, victims should initiate administrative recovery proceedings before the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) and the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

Every licensed recruiting agency (RL holder) in Bangladesh is required by law to maintain a substantial cash security deposit and bank guarantee with the government. When a formal complaint is submitted to the Director General of BMET detailing that an agency took money but failed to provide genuine visas, the BMET summons the agency managing director for a summary arbitration hearing. If the agency fails to refund the money, BMET has the statutory power to encash the agency's security deposit, disburse the funds directly to the victims, and suspend the agency's license on the government server.

sections.title: Bail Opposition and Compelling Financial Restitution
sections.content:
Because offenses under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 are strictly non-bailable, when the accused broker is arrested and produced before the Magistrate or Tribunal, their defense counsel routinely moves for bail. This is the pivotal moment in the litigation.

The victim's advocate must vigorously oppose bail, presenting the bank deposit slips and demonstrating that the accused defrauded poor migrant families of their life savings and that the stolen proceeds remain unrecovered. Because tribunals are exceptionally strict in human trafficking matters, bail is frequently denied. Facing prolonged incarceration in central jail, the accused broker's family is almost invariably compelled to approach the victim to negotiate an out-of-court settlement, refunding the full stolen amount via certified bank pay orders to secure conditional bail.

sections.title: Comparison Table: Human Trafficking (§2012) vs. Cheating (§420)
sections.content:
The table below summarizes the critical strategic advantages of prosecuting visa fraudsters under the Human Trafficking Act 2012 versus general cheating under the Penal Code:

ParameterHuman Trafficking Act 2012 (§7)Penal Code 1860 (Section 420 Cheating)
Punishment Severity7 years to Life Imprisonment + BDT 5L fineUp to 7 years imprisonment or fine
Bail ClassificationStrictly non-bailable (Hard to obtain)Non-bailable but bail granted routinely
Trial ForumSpecialized Anti-Human Trafficking TribunalRegular Magistrate / Assistant Sessions Court
Burden of ProofReverse burden on broker to prove legalityProsecution must prove every element
Compensation PowersCourt can order victim compensation directlyMust file separate civil Money Suit for money

Invoking the Human Trafficking Act 2012 transforms a slow civil dispute into a high-stakes criminal proceeding that prioritizes financial restitution.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 12 Lakh from a Visa Broker
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how specialized criminal prosecution recovered stolen migration funds in Tangail:

Two young brothers from Tangail wished to travel to Romania for warehouse employment. A local manpower broker in Dhaka promised them work permits and visas within four months, collecting BDT 12,00,000 across two bank transfers and two cash installments backed by handwritten money receipts. Six months passed without visas; the broker produced two suspicious PDF documents that Romanian embassy verification revealed were forged. When the brothers demanded their money back, the broker threatened to implicate them in false criminal cases through his political connections.

The brothers retained an advocate specializing in human trafficking litigation. The advocate bypasses general cheating charges and drafted a formal criminal complaint under Sections 3, 7, and 8 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012, filed directly before the Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal in Tangail. The petition annexed the bank transfer statements, handwritten receipts, and the embassy forgery confirmation. Concurrently, the advocate filed an administrative complaint before the Director General of BMET in Dhaka.

The Tribunal took immediate cognizance and issued non-bailable arrest warrants. Police arrested the broker at his Dhaka office and transferred him to Tangail jail. When the broker moved for bail, the brothers' advocate fiercely opposed it, highlighting the unrecovered BDT 12,00,000 and the life-destroying impact on the rural family. After two months in jail with multiple bail rejections, the broker's family approached the brothers: the broker paid the full BDT 12,00,000 back via three certified pay orders, achieving complete financial recovery and ending the family's nightmare.

faqs.question: Is taking money for a fake foreign visa considered human trafficking in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 3 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012, recruiting, transporting, or receiving money from any person for overseas employment through deception or fraudulent promises constitutes human trafficking.

faqs.question: What is the punishment for a visa broker (Dalal) under the Human Trafficking Act?
faqs.answer: Under Section 7 of the 2012 Act, human trafficking is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for not less than seven (7) years and up to life imprisonment, along with a mandatory fine of at least five lakh taka (BDT 5,00,000).

faqs.question: Can I get my money back from a fraudulent recruiting agency through BMET?
faqs.answer: Yes. Licensed recruiting agencies must maintain cash security deposits with the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare. If BMET finds the agency guilty of fraud during arbitration, it has the statutory power to forfeit the agency's security deposit and compensate victims directly.

faqs.question: What evidence is needed to prove visa fraud against an agent?
faqs.answer: You need bank transfer receipts, money receipts, WhatsApp chat messages, audio recordings of promises, passport copy handovers, and printouts of any fake visas or job appointment letters provided by the broker.

faqs.question: What should I do if the local police station refuses to file my case against a visa broker?
faqs.answer: If the local Thana refuses to register an FIR, your advocate can file a direct criminal petition before the specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal (Manob Pachar Daman Tribunal) in your district, which can issue direct arrest warrants.

faqs.question: Can an unlicensed sub-agent (Dalal) be prosecuted if they claim they gave the money to an agency?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 8 of the 2012 Act, abetting, assisting, or acting as an intermediary in human trafficking carries the same severe penalty. The sub-agent cannot escape liability by blaming an upstream agency.

faqs.question: How long does an Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunal case take in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under the 2012 Act, trials before Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunals are fast-tracked. Because offenses are strictly non-bailable, most fraudulent brokers seek an early financial compromise within 2 to 6 months of being remanded to custody.

faqs.question: Can an expatriate worker stranded abroad file a trafficking case in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. The stranded worker's family members in Bangladesh, or the worker acting through a Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy abroad, can file criminal cases against the recruiting syndicate in Bangladesh.
